sender.en: Someone you met on a dating app or social media

name.en: Online romance: someone you’ve never met asks for money

how.en: Someone you meet on a dating app or social media becomes very affectionate quickly and moves the chat to another app. They avoid video calls or meeting in person. In long-term scams they build a bond over months, then invent a crisis such as a medical, work or travel problem and ask for money, gift cards or crypto. In “romance baiting” the chat turns into a fake crypto or investment opportunity. They often tell you to keep it secret.

text.en: You meet someone online who says they love you very quickly.
They move the chat to another app and avoid video calls or meeting.
They ask you not to tell family or friends.
They have an emergency, or an investment tip, and ask for money, gift cards or crypto.
I’ve never felt this way about anyone. Let’s talk on WhatsApp, the app is not private. I can’t video call from the rig, the connection is too weak.
My love, they won’t release my equipment at customs until I pay the fee. I hate asking, but can you send $3,000? I’ll pay you back as soon as I’m home. Please don’t tell your family yet.

en: met someone on a dating app
asked me to send money for an emergency
online girlfriend asked for gift cards
he wants me to invest in crypto
my love needs money for customs
don't tell your family about us
They won’t video call or meet, or always cancel.
They want to move to a private messaging app.
Requests for money, gift cards, crypto, ID or account access.
They tell you to trust only them.
Never send money or personal details to someone you haven’t met in person.
Talk to a friend or family member about it. Do a reverse image search on their photos.
Save the messages, report the profile to the app and block them. If you sent money, contact your bank straight away.
